strengths: Novel representation of shape correspondences using invertible flows with elegant zero-shot capability through flow composition via shared Gaussian anchor - enables correspondence between any shape pair without retraining

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (FAUST, SMPL, SHREC20, Kinect) with diverse metrics (Euclidean, Geodesic, Dirichlet, coverage) and varied baselines from traditional to recent neural methods

Demonstrated versatility across different shape representations: naturally extends to point clouds, SDFs, and volumetric shapes with applications in parametrization, scan deformation, and inter-representation matching
Sound mathematical framework combining Conditional Flow Matching with well-motivated Gaussian anchor distributions; clear formulation with appropriate technical justification
Strong quantitative results generally outperforming or matching established baselines (Table 3), particularly on FAUST and point cloud datasets with often superior correspondence accuracy
Clear presentation with effective visualizations of the pipeline and qualitative results demonstrating correspondence quality across diverse scenarios
weaknesses: Fundamental smoothness limitations acknowledged in Section 5.1: flow inversion is non-smooth, contradicting claims about high-coverage correspondences; proposed post-hoc fixes (ZO, NAM) suggest the core method has inherent limitations not resolved by the main framework

Critical missing computational efficiency analysis: no runtime comparisons with baselines, unclear scalability with shape complexity and dataset size; for practical adoption, knowing whether FUSE is faster/slower than alternatives is essential

Embedding selection procedure (Section 4.3) appears ad-hoc without principled guidance; practitioners lack clear methodology for selecting embeddings for new problems; why some shapes benefit from Ours-zzO while others use WKS remains unexplained

Limited baseline comparisons with recent work: primarily compares against pre-2022 methods; while ZoomOut and NAM (2024) are mentioned, comprehensive comparison with other recent neural correspondence approaches from 2023-2024 is missing

Evaluation limited to relatively small-scale benchmarks: FAUST and SMPL are non-isometric human deformations only; SHREC20 contains only 14 animal shapes; missing large-scale diverse non-isometric collections by modern standards

Lack of statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing; Table 3 shows several methods with comparable performance - unclear if differences are statistically meaningful; only average results, no per-pair or per-category variance analysis

Application results primarily qualitative (Section 5.3): mesh parametrization and scan fitting lack quantitative metrics; volumetric matching shows comparable but not clearly superior results; applications feel somewhat disconnected from main contribution

Limited theoretical analysis: no justification for why Gaussian is optimal anchor or comparison with alternatives; lacks convergence analysis or approximation quality guarantees; relationship between embedding quality and correspondence performance not characterized
Reproducibility concerns: no code availability mentioned; network architecture details incomplete; training hyperparameters not fully justified; CFM simulation details insufficient for reproduction

Incomplete discussion of limitations (Section 6): lacks explicit treatment of failure cases, scenarios where method unsuitable, when zero-shot capability degrades, and memory/computational requirements for different problem scales

strengths: Novel flow-matching based approach for shape correspondence that elegantly composes mappings through a shared anchor distribution, providing a theoretically motivated framework
Impressive cross-modality generality supporting multiple 3D representations (meshes, point clouds, SDFs, volumetric data) without specialized modifications
Comprehensive experimental validation across four major benchmarks with multiple metrics, extensive baseline comparisons, and thorough ablation studies
Demonstrates practical versatility beyond shape matching through applications in human scan fitting, mesh parameterization, and volumetric correspondence
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and honest discussion of limitations; authors commit to code release for reproducibility
weaknesses: Method effectiveness critically depends on embedding quality—demonstrated degradation with embeddings lacking semantic structure (Fig. 5), fundamentally limiting robustness and automation
Requires manual placement of 5-6 landmarks per shape to handle intrinsic symmetries, making the approach labor-intensive and reducing practical applicability to fully automatic pipelines
Noticeably weaker performance on unstructured point clouds compared to mesh-based scenarios due to reliance on geodesic distances and surface coverage assumptions
Final KNN retrieval step compromises strict bijectivity despite continuous flow representations; discretization effects not fully characterized
FUSE maps exhibit lower smoothness than methods like FMaps with visible higher Dirichlet energy; smoothness-accuracy trade-off insufficiently explored
Computational complexity analysis is incomplete—training times underspecified, scaling behavior with shape complexity not rigorously analyzed despite claimed efficiency advantages
Results are competitive but rarely demonstrate clear superiority over simpler baselines; improvements often marginal in Table 4
No support for partial/incomplete shape matching, limiting applicability to practical scenarios with incomplete 3D scans
Limited formal theoretical justification for why flow composition preserves shape correspondence structure beyond empirical validation
